messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

It was a supply convoy, routine on paper, moving through open terrain in the early hours before the heat set in. Maya had been driving the lead vehicle, a role she had earned through steady competence and a quiet confidence that she could handle whatever came. What came was an IED buried in a patch of gravel that looked no different from the rest. The blast flipped the truck, and for what felt like an eternity, she was suspended upside down, the world a roar of twisted metal and dust, the smell of fuel and hot earth filling her lungs. She had to crawl out through the shattered windshield, her ears ringing, her vision swimming. She remembers the dizziness most of all—a deep, spinning disorientation that made the ground feel like it was tilting beneath her feet. She got everyone out, but something in her own footing never quite returned.

Now, two years later, Maya drives a city bus through the same kind of early-morning quiet. She is twenty-five, single, and lives alone in a small apartment. The job was supposed to be a return to normalcy, a way to prove she was still capable of moving people from one place to another. But the bus has become a cage of triggers. The unpredictable flow of traffic, a sudden brake from the car ahead, the way a passenger’s heavy bag can thump against the floor without warning—each jolt sends a ripple of dizziness through her skull. Stress builds throughout every shift, a low hum that spikes whenever she feels she cannot control what will happen next. Every time the bus lurches, she is back in that spinning cab, and she has come to believe that she is no longer capable of doing the things that defined her. The trauma, she is certain, has destroyed her life, leaving nothing that feels meaningful anymore.

The dizziness is the worst of it. It does not just remind her of the explosion; it convinces her that she is about to lose control again. When she feels lightheaded, she immediately scans the interior of the bus, checking every face, every exit, every possible threat. She has developed a rigid habit of driving with her back pressed against the driver’s seat as far as it will go, needing to feel that solid surface behind her so she can see the whole compartment. The more she scans, the more she finds to worry about—a man standing too close to the rear door, a teenager moving abruptly toward the front. Each perceived threat makes her feel weaker, more convinced that she is falling apart. This in turn makes her more sensitive to the next unpredictable jolt or dizzy spell, creating a loop that tightens with every block she drives. Her life feels meaningless now because she can no longer trust her own body or her own judgment, and that belief makes every unpredictable moment on the road feel like a confirmation of her failure.

She has started taking longer routes to avoid certain intersections where the road dips sharply, because the sensation of dropping makes her dizzy. She dreads rush hour, when the bus is full and the stops are unpredictable. At home, she sits with her back to a wall, watching the door. Nothing in her life feels meaningful anymore, and that emptiness makes her even more watchful, as if danger might be the only thing that still deserves her attention. She finally came to see a therapist because last week, she pulled over mid-route, her hands shaking, convinced she was about to pass out. She sat there for ten minutes, passengers growing impatient, and she realized she could not go on pretending she was okay. What frightens her most is not the memory of the blast itself, but the growing certainty that she will never feel steady again.
